analogy.p: A plant is like a castle. The thick walls and moat are the cellulose cell walls and waxy cuticle (physical defences). The boiling oil and poison on the wall are the antibacterial chemicals and poisons (chemical defences). The spikes and the drawbridge that lifts are the thorns and drooping leaves (mechanical defences). Scouts who identify the attackers are like laboratory tests and antibody kits. It breaks down because a castle is built by people and cannot grow or repair itself, whereas a plant grows and replaces damaged tissue.

bullets: **Detection** is by looking for symptoms: **stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay (rot), growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration and the presence of pests**.
**Identification** can use a **gardening manual or website**, **laboratory testing** to identify the pathogen, or **testing kits that contain monoclonal antibodies**.
Plants can be infected by a range of **viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens** as well as by **insects**.
**Ion deficiencies** (for example nitrate or magnesium) also cause disease-like symptoms.
Plants have **physical, chemical and mechanical** adaptations that defend against attack.
Plant diseases matter because they cut crop yield and can threaten food security.
core.p: This is a **triple (separate science) only** point in AQA 4.3 Infection and response. You must be able to **describe how plant diseases are detected and identified**, name the symptoms and the possible causes (viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens, insects and **mineral ion deficiencies**), and describe the **physical, chemical and mechanical defences** that plants have against disease and attack. It links to photosynthesis, mineral ions in plant nutrition and pathogens in humans.

bullets: Reduced photosynthesis means **less glucose** for respiration, growth and making biomass.
Disease can cause **crop failure**, economic loss and shortage of food, especially where one crop is relied on.
Pathogens spread by wind, water, soil, contact and by **insect vectors** such as aphids.
Identifying the exact cause matters because the **correct treatment** depends on whether the problem is a virus, fungus, pest or lack of minerals.
Link to other topics: communicable disease in humans (4.3), photosynthesis (4.4), food security (4.7).
core.p: Plants are the producers in food chains, and crops feed people and livestock. A plant disease reduces growth, yield or quality, and some can spread across large areas. Diseased leaves cannot photosynthesise well, so less glucose is made for growth and storage. Quick, accurate detection allows farmers and gardeners to treat or isolate plants before the disease spreads.

bullets: **Stunted growth**: the plant is smaller than normal.
**Spots on leaves**: discoloured patches of different colours and sizes.
**Areas of decay (rot)**: parts of the plant tissue break down and die.
**Growths**: abnormal lumps or swellings on stems, roots or leaves.
**Malformed stems or leaves**: distorted, curled or abnormal shapes.
**Discolouration**: leaves that are yellow, pale or patterned instead of green.
**Presence of pests**: insects or signs of their damage on the plant.
core.p: The first step is to look carefully at the plant. Symptoms are the visible signs that something is wrong. Listing the symptoms accurately is the basis for deciding on the cause. Examiners expect you to recall the exact symptom list from the specification.

bullets: **Laboratory testing** of a sample can identify the actual **pathogen** present (for example under a microscope or by culturing it), which gives high accuracy.
**Testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies** detect specific antigens of a pathogen; the antibody binds only to the matching pathogen, so a positive result shows which disease is present.
Experts may also check for **mineral ion deficiency** by comparing the symptoms with known deficiency symptoms or testing the soil.
The more accurate a method, the better the decision about **treatment**.
core.p: Symptoms alone can be shared by different problems, so the cause must be identified. This is done in three main ways, each with advantages: speed, cost and certainty. **Gardening manuals or websites** let a gardener compare symptoms with pictures and descriptions; quick and cheap but not certain.

bullets: **Viral**: a virus enters plant cells and reproduces, damaging cells. Example: **tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)** causes a mosaic of discoloured leaves, which reduces photosynthesis and stunts growth.

**Fungal**: fungi grow on or in the plant. Example: **rose black spot** causes purple or black spots on leaves, which then turn yellow and fall off, so less photosynthesis occurs. It is spread by the wind and water and treated with fungicides and by stripping affected leaves.
**Bacterial**: bacteria multiply in plant tissues and can cause rot, spots or growths.
**Insect pests**: for example **aphids** feed on plant sap and can spread viruses from plant to plant.
Pathogens are named by type in questions: you may be asked to link a described symptom to a likely type of cause.
core.p: Plant diseases are caused by the same broad groups of pathogens as human diseases, plus pests that feed on the plant. A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes disease. Different groups spread and damage plants in different ways and need different treatments.

bullets: Nitrate ions are absorbed by roots (by active transport) from soil water.
Nitrate is used to make **amino acids and then proteins**, so is essential for growth.
**Deficiency symptom: stunted growth.** Older leaves may also turn pale or yellow.
Fertilisers containing nitrates are added to soil to replace nitrate removed by crops.
The reason is always the link: **no nitrate, no protein synthesis, so poor growth**.
core.p: Plants take in mineral ions through their roots from the soil. If a mineral is missing, the plant cannot make something it needs and develops deficiency symptoms. **Nitrate ions** are needed to make **amino acids**, which are joined to make **proteins**. Proteins are needed for **growth** (new cells and enzymes).

bullets: Magnesium ions are taken up from the soil by the roots.
They are a part of the **chlorophyll molecule**, so they are essential for making it.
**Deficiency symptom: chlorosis** (yellowing of leaves, especially the leaf tissue between veins).
Less chlorophyll means **less light absorbed**, so **less photosynthesis**, so less glucose and slower growth.
Link to other topics: photosynthesis (limiting factors) and mineral ions in plant nutrition.
core.p: **Magnesium ions** are needed to make **chlorophyll**, the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Without enough magnesium, leaves cannot make enough chlorophyll and become yellow, a condition called **chlorosis**.

bullets: **Cellulose cell walls** around plant cells form a strong barrier that pathogens must break through.
A **tough waxy cuticle** on the leaves is a waterproof layer that pathogens find hard to penetrate and that makes water run off the leaf.
**Layers of dead cells around stems** form **bark** on trees, which provides a barrier; these cells **fall off** and take with them any pathogens that have settled there.
These defences work like human skin, which is also a barrier against pathogens.
They are **always present**, whether or not the plant is under attack.
core.p: Physical defences are barriers that stop pathogens getting into the plant in the first place. If the barrier is broken, microbes can enter and cause disease, so these barriers are the first line of defence.

bullets: Some plants make **poisons that deter herbivores** (animals that eat plants), so they are not eaten.
Chemicals may be present all the time or made when the plant is attacked.
Examples you can use include chemicals in some plants that are poisonous to insects or grazing animals.
Link to other topics: many drugs, such as digitalis from foxglove, come from these chemicals.
core.p: Plants make chemicals that kill or discourage pathogens and animals. Many of these chemicals later became sources of human drugs, which links back to the discovery of drugs from plants. Plants produce **antibacterial chemicals** that kill bacteria.

bullets: **Leaves that droop or curl when touched** can remove insects from the plant or make the plant a less attractive target.
**Mimicry** is where a plant copies the appearance of another thing to trick animals, for example looking like it is already damaged or has insect eggs so insects do not lay eggs on it.
These adaptations reduce animal damage and so reduce the chance of infection through wounds.
In exams, sort defences correctly into the three groups: physical, chemical or mechanical.
core.p: Mechanical adaptations are structural features or movements that protect plants from being eaten or damaged by animals. They stop the damage that would also let pathogens in. **Thorns and hairs** on leaves and stems deter animals from touching or eating the plant.

bullets: **Stunted growth** with no obvious spots suggests **nitrate deficiency** (or a virus).
**Mosaic pattern** of light and dark patches on leaves suggests **a virus such as TMV**.
**Black or purple spots** that spread and leaves falling suggest **fungal black spot**.
**Insects visible on the plant** suggest a pest such as aphids; they can also carry viruses.
To be certain you need identification by a **laboratory test or monoclonal antibody kit**.
core.p: A frequent exam skill is to read a description or table of symptoms and decide whether they point to a pathogen, a pest or a mineral deficiency. Use the clue and give the reason. Yellow leaves with **veins still green** suggest **chlorosis** and **magnesium deficiency**.

exam: **List the symptoms (up to 3 marks)**: stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay, growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, pests. Give one per mark.
**How can a plant disease be identified? (2 to 3 marks)**: gardening manual or website; laboratory testing to identify the pathogen; testing kits containing monoclonal antibodies.
**Explain a deficiency (2 to 3 marks)**: always give the three-step link, for example: magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so less light is absorbed, so less photosynthesis and yellow leaves.
**Nitrate question**: nitrates are needed to make amino acids and proteins, so growth is poor (stunted).
**Classify defences**: put each under physical, chemical or mechanical; do not mix them up.
**Describe physical defences (3 marks)**: cellulose cell walls; waxy cuticle; layers of dead cells (bark) that fall off.
**Why does a diseased leaf make less food? (2 marks)**: less photosynthesis because spots or lack of chlorophyll reduce light absorption.
**Data question on fertiliser trials**: compare plants with and without the mineral; quote figures and state the effect on growth.
**Use 'because'** in every explain question so you link cause to effect.
**Compare with humans**: the waxy cuticle and bark are like skin, so a comparison with the human defences can be credited.

mistakes.r: Lack of nitrate ions causes stunted growth (not enough protein); lack of magnesium causes chlorosis.
mistakes.w: Stunted growth is caused by a lack of magnesium.

mistakes.r: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, which is the green pigment.
mistakes.w: Magnesium makes leaves green because it is a colour.

mistakes.r: Plants have a cellulose cell wall, a waxy cuticle and dead cell layers (bark) as physical barriers.
Thorns, hairs, drooping leaves and mimicry are mechanical adaptations.
mistakes.w: Mimicry and thorns are chemical defences.

mistakes.r: Aphids are insect pests; pathogens are microorganisms such as viruses, bacteria and fungi.
In plant testing kits they detect and identify the pathogen; they are not a treatment.
mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies cure the plant disease.

mistakes.r: Yellow leaves could be a virus or chlorosis from magnesium deficiency; use other symptoms to decide.
mistakes.w: Yellow leaves always mean a virus.

mistakes.r: Layers of dead cells around stems form a barrier and fall off, taking pathogens with them.
mistakes.w: Dead cell layers are a weakness.

summary: You need to know how plant diseases are detected (symptoms) and identified (manuals, laboratory tests, monoclonal antibody kits), the causes (viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens, insects and nitrate or magnesium deficiency) and the physical, chemical and mechanical defences of plants. It matters because plant disease reduces photosynthesis and crop yield and threatens food supply.

terms.d: A visible sign that something is wrong with the plant, for example spots or stunted growth.
Growth that is smaller than normal.
Yellowing of leaves because of too little chlorophyll, caused by magnesium deficiency.
Mineral ions absorbed from soil and used to make amino acids and proteins.
Mineral ions needed to make chlorophyll.
A lack of a mineral ion in the soil so the plant cannot make substances it needs.
An antibody from one clone of cells that binds to one specific antigen, used in testing kits to identify a pathogen.
A virus that causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis.
A fungal disease causing purple or black spots on leaves, which then yellow and fall off.
An insect pest that feeds on plant sap and can spread viruses.
A strong wall around plant cells that acts as a physical barrier to pathogens.
A tough waterproof layer on the leaf surface that acts as a barrier.
A mechanical adaptation where a plant looks like something else to trick animals.
A chemical used to kill fungi.

worked.ans: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll. With too little magnesium the plant makes less chlorophyll, so the leaves turn yellow (chlorosis) and less light is absorbed for photosynthesis, so the plant grows poorly.
worked.q: A gardener finds yellow leaves on a plant. Explain how magnesium deficiency causes this. (3 marks)
steps: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll.
Without enough magnesium, chlorophyll cannot be made, so leaves become yellow (chlorosis).
Less light is absorbed so less photosynthesis occurs.

worked.ans: A tough waxy cuticle and cellulose cell walls act as physical barriers to pathogens. Plants make antibacterial chemicals and poisons that deter herbivores. Thorns and hairs, or leaves that curl when touched, are mechanical defences that stop animals eating the plant.
worked.q: Describe three ways in which a plant defends itself against pathogens or being eaten. (3 marks)
steps: Physical: cellulose cell wall or waxy cuticle or bark.
Mechanical: thorns, hairs, drooping leaves or mimicry.

worked.ans: The likely cause is a viral infection such as tobacco mosaic virus. It can be confirmed by a laboratory test of a sample or by a testing kit containing monoclonal antibodies that bind to the virus.
worked.q: A farmer sees plants with a mosaic pattern of light and dark green on the leaves. Suggest the likely cause and how to confirm it. (3 marks)
steps: Mosaic pattern is a typical symptom of a virus such as tobacco mosaic virus.
Confirm by laboratory testing to identify the pathogen.
Or use a testing kit that contains monoclonal antibodies.
